ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State

Ze-Wei Liou1, Harris Nover2, Amey Naik2, Andrii Skliar2 Igor Shovkun2, Ido Shahaf2, Tri Dao1 1Princeton University  2NVIDIA {zewei.liou, tridao}@princeton.edu
{hnover, ameyn, askliar, ishovkun, ishahaf}@nvidia.com
Abstract

State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by 1.201.20–1.47×1.47\times over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about 1.8×1.8\times the throughput of vLLM’s speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.

Code: https://github.com/Johnny-Liou/ReplaySSM.

1 Introduction

Long chain-of-thought reasoning makes decoding a substantial cost in LLM inference. Agent workloads stretch it further through repeated tool calls and reasoning. Transformer attention keeps past keys and values in a key-value (KV) cache whose size and per-step memory traffic grow with sequence length, hurting both throughput and tail latency. State-space models (SSMs), such as Mamba-2 (Dao & Gu, 2024), Gated DeltaNet (GDN; Yang et al., 2025), and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA; Kimi Team, 2025), instead summarize past information into a fixed-size recurrent state. Their state storage and per-step memory traffic remain constant with sequence length, but this compression can degrade exact recall (Jelassi et al., 2024; Waleffe et al., 2024). Hybrid architectures aim to find the sweet spot in between by interleaving SSM and attention layers and are widely adopted in production models, including Nemotron-3 (NVIDIA, 2025), Qwen3.5 through Qwen3.8 (Qwen Team, 2026a; Qwen Team, 2026b), Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), and GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026a).

A fixed-size state, however, does not make SSM decoding cheap. Current SSM decoding follows the recurrence step by step. Each step loads the state, updates it, computes the output from the updated state, and stores it back. This leads to three challenges. First, the update has low arithmetic intensity. Each step moves the full state for a decay and a rank-1 update. At serving batch sizes, this state traffic can make SSM updates the bottleneck up to 100K tokens even in hybrid models whose attention cost grows with output context length (Figure 1, bottom left). Second, an updated state has no cheap rollback. This becomes a problem for speculative decoding, which verifies multiple draft tokens together and must restore the state to the last accepted token when a suffix is rejected (Leviathan et al., 2023). Serving systems such as vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) therefore work around this by storing a separate recurrent-state snapshot for each draft token. These writes slow an already memory-bound kernel, and storing the snapshots caps concurrency, so speculative decoding gains little at serving batch sizes. Third, quantizing the SSM state feeds rounding error into subsequent recurrent updates, where it can accumulate over a long generation. Aggressively reducing state precision can therefore distort the output distribution and degrade downstream accuracy.

These three challenges motivate the question: Why do we store an updated state after every step? Unrolling the recurrence shows that the current state equals a decayed earlier checkpoint plus a short sum over recent inputs. ReplaySSM therefore represents the state as a checkpoint and a bounded buffer of recent SSM inputs (Figure 1, top). This representation separates output computation from checkpoint updates. On most steps (non-flush steps), ReplaySSM appends the new inputs to the buffer and computes the output from the checkpoint and the buffer without storing a state. Only when the buffer fills (flush steps) does it fold the buffered inputs into the checkpoint and start a new window. The outputs match conventional decoding up to floating-point differences.

This separation addresses all three challenges. A non-flush step writes only the new input vectors and decay factors, which are far smaller than the state, so checkpoint writes are amortized over the window and the dominant state traffic roughly halves. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback cheap. Rejected draft tokens are discarded by moving a buffer pointer, and because non-flush steps need only outputs, verification can compute them directly from the checkpoint and the cached inputs without materializing intermediate states. For low-precision states, the two roles can use different precisions: a low-precision checkpoint serves output computation on non-flush steps, while a higher-precision checkpoint carries the recurrence across flushes, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce ReplaySSM, which represents the SSM state as a checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs, separating output computation from checkpoint updates and avoiding full-state writes on most decoding steps (Section 4).

  • •

    We extend it to speculative decoding, where the cached inputs give pointer-based rollback and output-only verification (Section 5).

  • •

    We extend it to low-precision state storage, where the separation lets output computation and recurrent updates use different state precisions (Section 6).

  • •

    We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and GDN. At serving batch size 256, it speeds up standard decoding by 1.201.20–1.47×1.47\times over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about 1.8×1.8\times the throughput of vLLM’s speculative decoding on the two 120B-class mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Separate state precisions also reduce output Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint (Section 7).

2 Preliminaries

2.1 State-Space Models

SSMs compress the token history into a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing KV cache. In Mamba-2, the recurrence is

St=αt​St−1+vt​kt⊤,ot=St​qt,S_{t}=\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}+v_{t}k_{t}^{\top},\qquad o_{t}=S_{t}q_{t}, (1)

where St∈ℝdv×dkS_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{k}} is the state, vt,ot∈ℝdvv_{t},o_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}, kt,qt∈ℝdkk_{t},q_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, and αt∈(0,1)\alpha_{t}\in(0,1) is a data-dependent scalar decay. We write γi:j=∏ℓ=ijαℓ\gamma_{i:j}=\prod_{\ell=i}^{j}\alpha_{\ell} for the cumulative decay, with γi:j=1\gamma_{i:j}=1 when i>ji>j, and abbreviate γ1:h\gamma_{1:h} as γh\gamma_{h}. Each step loads St−1S_{t-1} from HBM, forms StS_{t} and oto_{t}, and stores StS_{t} back.

Delta-rule models such as GDN and KDA modify stored information before writing new information. The GDN recurrence is

St=αt​St−1​(I−βt​kt​kt⊤)+βt​vt​kt⊤,S_{t}=\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}\left(I-\beta_{t}k_{t}k_{t}^{\top}\right)+\beta_{t}v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}, (2)

where βt∈(0,1)\beta_{t}\in(0,1) controls the write strength. With

ut=βt​(vt−αt​St−1​kt)it becomesSt=αt​St−1+ut​kt⊤,u_{t}=\beta_{t}\left(v_{t}-\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}k_{t}\right)\qquad\text{it becomes}\qquad S_{t}=\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}+u_{t}k_{t}^{\top}, (3)

the same outer-product form as Mamba-2 with utu_{t} in place of vtv_{t}, at the cost of computing utu_{t} from the previous state.

2.2 Speculative Decoding and Quantization

Speculative decoding uses a lightweight drafter to propose multiple candidate tokens, which the target model verifies in one forward pass; how many are accepted is known only after this pass. Rejected tokens are discarded, and the KV cache or SSM state must retain only the accepted prefix (Leviathan et al., 2023). Quantization stores values in a lower-precision format to cut storage and memory traffic. Values the format cannot represent are rounded: round-to-nearest (RTN) can introduce systematic bias, while stochastic rounding (SR) is unbiased in expectation but still has nonzero variance (Gupta et al., 2015; Croci et al., 2022).

3 Motivation and Key Insight

SSMs compress an O⁡(N)O(N)-token history into an O⁡(1)O(1)-size state through recurrent updates. However, directly and eagerly following the recurrence, materializing the updated state at every decoding step, creates three challenges (Figure 1, bottom): low arithmetic intensity, expensive rollback, and propagation of quantization error through the recurrence.

3.1 Challenge 1: Large State I/O with Little Compute

Conventional decoding reads and writes the full recurrent state at each step while doing little computation on it; Mamba-2, for example, applies only an elementwise decay and a rank-1 update. State updates are therefore memory-bound, and state I/O dominates their latency (Appendix C.1). One might expect attention to dominate hybrid-model latency because its KV-cache traffic grows with context length. However, for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4 at batch size 256 on one B300, SSM state updates remain the largest latency component up to 100K tokens (Figure 1, bottom left). Two factors explain this. The model has five times as many SSM layers as attention layers, and each SSM layer’s FP32 state is 4 MiB per sequence, the size of an attention layer’s FP8 KV cache for 8K tokens. A decoding step loads and stores the state but only loads the KV cache, so the SSM layers move more bytes than the attention layers until the context reaches about 80K tokens (Appendix C.2). The measured crossover near 100K tokens is consistent with attention kernels having received more optimization effort (Dao et al., 2022, e.g.,).

3.2 Challenge 2: Recurrent State Has No Cheap Rollback

Conventional SSM decoding eagerly summarizes each token’s inputs into the state at once, and the update has no cheap inverse. This matters for speculative decoding, where the target model must roll the state back when it rejects a suffix of draft tokens (Figure 1, bottom middle). Attention handles rollback naturally by moving the KV-cache pointer to the end of the accepted prefix. An SSM state contains no token history to point into, so serving systems such as vLLM store a state snapshot for each draft token and select the one matching the accepted prefix. Verifying TT tokens costs TT full-state writes per step on an already memory-bound path and reduces serving concurrency. Prior work (Wang et al., 2024a; Wu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026; Section 8) avoids the per-token snapshots but still pays extra state traffic to recover the accepted state by re-running the recurrence, and at a serving batch size none of it is more than a few percent faster than vLLM’s snapshots (Appendix A). Speculative decoding therefore gives SSMs little speedup at serving batch sizes.

3.3 Challenge 3: Quantization Error Propagates Through Recurrence

In low-precision SSM decoding, the stored quantized state both produces the current output and feeds the next recurrent update. Rounding error therefore re-enters the recurrence at every step and can accumulate with sequence length (Figure 1, bottom right). Round-to-nearest adds systematic bias; stochastic rounding is unbiased but still propagates its variance (Appendix C.6).

3.4 ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State

All three problems come from one state-management policy: eagerly summarize each token’s inputs into the state at once and write the state to HBM at every step. The recurrence itself shows that this is unnecessary. For Mamba-2, let SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} be the state before a window of hh inputs indexed locally by j=1,…,hj=1,\ldots,h. Then

St=αtSt−1+vtkt⊤=γhSckpt+∑j=1hγj+1:hvjkj⊤.S_{t}=\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}+v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}=\gamma_{h}S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\gamma_{j+1:h}v_{j}k_{j}^{\top}. (4)

The recurrent form loads the summary St−1S_{t-1} and applies the current inputs; the unrolled form reconstructs the same state from SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} and the recent inputs {(αj,vj,kj)}j=1h\{(\alpha_{j},v_{j},k_{j})\}_{j=1}^{h}. Delta-rule models unroll the same way (Appendix B.1) once their updates are written in outer-product form (Equation 3).

ReplaySSM therefore represents the state as a checkpoint SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} plus a bounded buffer ℬ\mathcal{B} of recent SSM inputs; for Mamba-2 each record holds (αj,vj,kj)(\alpha_{j},v_{j},k_{j}). This representation separates output computation from checkpoint updates. Conventional decoding fuses the two, because the output is read from the state it has just updated and must store for the next step. A non-flush step appends the current inputs to ℬ\mathcal{B} and computes the output from SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} and the buffer without storing a state. When the buffer reaches its capacity, a flush step folds the buffered inputs into SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}}, computes the output, writes the new checkpoint to HBM, and clears the buffer. State writes therefore happen only on flush steps, and the outputs equal those of conventional decoding up to floating-point differences (Figure 1). Sections 4 to 6 build on this separation for standard decoding, speculative decoding, and low-precision state, and Section 8 reviews related work.

4 ReplaySSM for Standard Decoding

Standard decoding is the simplest setting in which to see how the separation reduces state memory traffic (Challenge 1). The core operation reconstructs the current state from a checkpoint and the cached inputs. For a checkpoint SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} and replay buffer ℬ1:h={(αj,vj,kj)}j=1h\mathcal{B}_{1:h}=\{(\alpha_{j},v_{j},k_{j})\}_{j=1}^{h}, define

Replay(Sckpt,ℬ1:h)=γhSckpt+∑j=1hγj+1:hvjkj⊤.\textsc{Replay}(S_{\mathrm{ckpt}},\mathcal{B}_{1:h})=\gamma_{h}S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\gamma_{j+1:h}v_{j}k_{j}^{\top}. (5)

Algorithm 4 applies this operation once per token. Lines 1–3 append the current inputs, reconstruct the state, and compute the output; the only full-state store is Line 5, inside the flush branch. Algorithms 4 and 4 extend it in Sections 5 and 6. For GDN, each record stores the correction uju_{j} in place of vjv_{j} and the flush replays the same sum (Appendix B.2).

Conventional decoding reads and writes the full recurrent state at every step. ReplaySSM still reads SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} at each step, since the output computation needs it, but writes the state only when the checkpoint is updated. A non-flush step only appends the current inputs to ℬ\mathcal{B}. Over an LL-step window, both methods perform LL full-state reads, while conventional decoding performs LL full-state writes and ReplaySSM performs one, plus the buffer reads and writes. Because the buffer is much smaller than the state, ReplaySSM roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic (Appendix C.3).

The window size LL balances checkpoint writes against replay overhead. A larger LL amortizes each checkpoint write over more steps but increases the number of buffered inputs loaded and applied at each step. We use L=16L=16 throughout (Appendix C.5).

5 ReplaySSM for Speculative Decoding

In speculative decoding, ReplaySSM keeps the traffic saving of standard decoding (Section 4) and changes how the target model verifies draft tokens in two further ways: cached inputs make rollback cheap, and output-only evaluation avoids materializing intermediate recurrent states.

5.1 Cheap Rollback with Cached Inputs

The accepted-prefix length is known only after target-model verification (Section 2.2). ReplaySSM therefore appends the SSM inputs of all TT tokens of the verification pass to the replay buffer first and commits only the accepted prefix after verification by moving the buffer pointer. Algorithm 4 gives the procedure for Mamba-2. The draft records are written after the hh committed records (Line 1), and all h+Th+T records feed the output computation (Line 3). The accepted length aa is known only after the outputs are returned (Line 9), and it then advances hh (Line 10). Rejected records lie beyond position hh and are overwritten by the next append. The flush branch (Lines 4–8) folds only committed inputs into the checkpoint, so it can run before acceptance is known. Non-flush steps write only the small input records, and only flush steps write the checkpoint. Appendix A compares the per-step state traffic with vLLM’s per-draft snapshots and with the prior recovery methods of Section 3.2.

We implement ℬ\mathcal{B} as a circular buffer with capacity L+TL+T, room for LL committed records and TT drafts, so dropping the committed prefix (Line 8) advances the ring origin instead of copying the draft records forward. Flushing when h+T>Lh+T>L keeps the committed length at most LL after verification (Appendix D.1). Unlike the fixed LL-step interval of standard decoding, the flush frequency now depends on acceptance, since higher acceptance fills the buffer faster.

5.2 Output-Only Verification

The separation also lets a non-flush step avoid materializing the state as well as storing it. Conventional decoding must produce the updated state because the next step consumes it. Under ReplaySSM no later step reads the state of a non-flush step, so that step needs only the output. For a single Mamba-2 update from a zero state, the product of vv, k⊤k^{\top}, and qq can be bracketed two ways, o=(v​k⊤)​q=v⁡(k⊤​q)o=(vk^{\top})q=v(k^{\top}q): the left side materializes the dv×dkd_{v}\times d_{k} state, while the right side forms the scalar k⊤​qk^{\top}q and scales vv. We call the right-hand form output-only evaluation.

For verification, let VV and KK hold the h+Th+T buffered values and keys as columns, committed records first, and let Q=[q1,…,qT]Q=[q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}]. The same idea gives

OutputOnly(Sckpt,ℬ1:h+T,Q)=SckptQD+V(W⊙(K⊤Q)),\textsc{OutputOnly}(S_{\mathrm{ckpt}},\mathcal{B}_{1:h+T},Q)=S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}QD+V\bigl(W\odot(K^{\top}Q)\bigr), (6)

where DD is diagonal with Ds​s=γh+sD_{ss}=\gamma_{h+s}, ⊙\odot is the elementwise product, and WW holds cumulative decays under a causal mask, Wj​s=γj+1:h+sW_{js}=\gamma_{j+1:h+s} for j≤h+sj\leq h+s and 00 otherwise. The mask restricts each draft query to the committed history and the drafts up to its own position. The output-only form has two benefits. It never materializes a state, so it needs fewer FLOPs (Appendix C.4), and K⊤​QK^{\top}Q is computed once for every group of value heads that share keys and queries. Both matter more in speculative decoding, where verifying TT tokens multiplies the arithmetic per step. The outputs match recurrent evaluation up to floating-point differences. GDN admits the same form. Its draft corrections depend on the earlier drafts in the window, and Appendix B.3 obtains all TT of them from one T×TT\times T triangular solve. Equation 6 also has the chunkwise form of prefill and training kernels, with the buffered inputs followed by the drafts as the chunk (Section 8).

6 ReplaySSM for Low-Precision State

Lower-precision state storage reduces memory traffic and can reduce latency in memory-bound SSM kernels. In conventional decoding the same stored state computes the output and feeds the next update, so its rounding error re-enters the recurrence at every step (Section 3.3). The separation changes this in two ways. It quantizes the state once per window instead of once per step, though with a single low-precision checkpoint that rounding error still enters later updates. More important, non-flush steps read the state only to compute outputs, while flush steps update the checkpoint that carries the recurrence forward, so the two roles can use different precisions.

We therefore keep a high-precision checkpoint SckptHPS_{\mathrm{ckpt}}^{\mathrm{HP}} for recurrent updates and a low-precision copy SckptLPS_{\mathrm{ckpt}}^{\mathrm{LP}} for non-flush output computation. Both represent the same checkpoint history; 𝒬HP\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{HP}} and 𝒬LP\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{LP}} denote the casts from accumulation precision. Algorithm 4 extends Algorithm 4 by choosing which checkpoint to load (Lines 2–3). Non-flush steps read the low-precision copy. Flush steps read the high-precision checkpoint, reconstruct the committed state, and cast it independently into both formats (Lines 7–8). The extra low-precision write on flush steps lets every non-flush step read the smaller checkpoint. Acceptance, rollback, and buffer management are unchanged.

Separate precisions break the feedback loop of Section 3.3. Each flush starts from the high-precision checkpoint and writes a fresh high-precision checkpoint; the low-precision copy is derived from it and never read back into the recurrence, so its rounding error does not accumulate. Rounding error in the high-precision path remains, and non-flush outputs still depend on the approximate copy. Appendix C.6 provides the analysis, and Section 7.4 measures the resulting output error as KL divergence. GDN needs one adjustment. The corrections uu cached on non-flush steps come from the low-precision checkpoint (Equation 3), so we also cache vv and recompute the corrections from the high-precision state at flush time, keeping low-precision error out of the recurrence (Appendix B.4).

7 Evaluation

7.1 Setup

We evaluate four hybrid models from two families, Nemotron-3 with Mamba-2 layers and Qwen3.5 with GDN layers (Table 1), each on one GPU without tensor parallelism. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM (Appendix D) and compare against tuned conventional vLLM decoding with CUDA graphs. All performance experiments store the recurrent state in FP32, the default for all four models. Section 7.4 lowers only the state precision and leaves weights as released (Table 1). We write BB for batch size, LL for the replay window size, TT for the verification length, the tokens verified per step (T=1T=1 is standard decoding), aa for the number of those tokens it commits, 1≤a≤T1\leq a\leq T, and NN for generation length. Standard decoding reports whole-model latency per decode step and standalone SSM-kernel latency. Speculative decoding reports serving throughput in generated tokens per second, prefill included, and standalone kernel latency for verification. The low-precision experiments measure the KL divergence DKL(pFP32∥pconfig)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{FP32}}\|p_{\mathrm{config}}) from conventional FP32-state decoding under teacher forcing on PG-19 (Rae et al., 2019) for NN up to 128K tokens, and generated-answer accuracy on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024b), GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2023), and the Level 5 subset of MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), Math-L5. Details are in Appendix E.1.

7.2 Standard Decoding

The baseline uses the fastest kernel launch configuration for each model, which beats the shipped Mamba-2 defaults (Appendix E.2.1). At B=256B=256 and L=16L=16, ReplaySSM speeds up the SSM kernel by 1.461.46–1.80×1.80\times and the whole decode step by 1.201.20–1.47×1.47\times across the four models (Figure 1). The kernel gain is the traffic reduction of Section 4 and appears where the conventional kernel is memory-bound. Appendix E.2.1 sweeps the batch size from 1 to 512 and reports the HBM bandwidth the conventional kernel reaches. At B=1B=1, the kernel is latency-bound, and ReplaySSM ends within a few percent of the baseline end to end. From there the speedup grows with batch size until the conventional kernel saturates the bandwidth. The end-to-end gain is bounded by the SSM share of the decode step, since attention and the rest of the model are unchanged, and it also grows with batch size because that share grows. We use L=16L=16 because it gives the lowest amortized kernel latency for all four models at B=256B=256 in the window sweep of Appendix E.2.2, which the traffic analysis of Appendix C.5 also predicts.

7.3 Speculative Decoding

We evaluate the two 120B-class models, which run with NVFP4 weights (Table 1), at L=16L=16 and T=4T=4, drafting with each model’s MTP head on GSM8K prompts (Cobbe et al., 2021) with 256 generated tokens per request. Figure 4 compares serving throughput with conventional vLLM standard and speculative decoding. Storing a state snapshot per draft token adds O⁡(T)O(T) state writes per step and caps the concurrency that GPU memory allows, so conventional speculation stops gaining beyond B=128B=128 and on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B at B=512B=512 falls below standard decoding. ReplaySSM keeps improving with batch size. At B=512B=512 it delivers 1.85×1.85\times and 2.10×2.10\times the throughput of conventional speculation, and 2.16×2.16\times and 1.90×1.90\times that of standard decoding, with matched acceptance lengths. Appendix E.3 gives the serving setup, the throughput over the full grid of BB and TT, and the acceptance lengths. The faster verification kernel is the other source of the gain. Figure 4 shows its cost on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B at B=256B=256. Conventional verification stores one snapshot per token, so its latency grows with TT and reaches 4.66×4.66\times a standard-decoding step at T=8T=8. ReplaySSM verifies eight tokens for 0.890.89–1.21×1.21\times of a standard step, flushes included. The band spans all drafts rejected to all accepted, since higher acceptance fills the buffer and flushes more often. The GDN kernel shows the same trend (Appendix E.3.2).

7.4 Low-Precision State

A low-precision state reduces latency (Appendix E.4.2) but can distort the output distribution and degrade downstream accuracy. We compare a shared checkpoint (FP32, FP16, FP8, or NVFP4) that serves both output computation and recurrent updates against separate read and recurrence checkpoints (FP8 or NVFP4 reads with FP32 or FP16 recurrence under stochastic rounding, SR), all at L=16L=16 and with the formats of Appendix E.4.1. Quantization applies to decoding only, and prefill computes the state at full precision. These runs use standard decoding. Speculative decoding changes how many tokens a step verifies, and acceptance sets when flushes occur. Neither changes which values are rounded, so the error mechanism is the same. Figure 6 shows the output KL from FP32-state decoding on Qwen3.5-4B. Shared FP8 and NVFP4 checkpoints accumulate error with generation length, as Section 3.3 describes, and keeping the recurrence in FP32 removes most of it. At 128K tokens, NVFP4 reads with FP32 recurrence reduce KL from 0.136 to 0.0038, about 36×36\times. What remains is the read error itself, which does not grow with NN but keeps NVFP4 reads several times above the FP32 floor. FP16+SR recurrence tracks FP32 recurrence closely, so a half-precision recurrence checkpoint suffices, and we use it in the accuracy evaluation. Appendix E.4.3 gives the KL protocol and the curves of the other three models, which show the same separation by model-dependent amounts. Appendix E.4.4 varies LL. A shared checkpoint is requantized once per window, so its error falls as LL grows (Section 6), while the separate configurations are nearly unchanged.

Table 2 shows the downstream consequence, with separate rows listing read / recurrence precision. A shared NVFP4+SR checkpoint loses 13.05 points of GPQA-Diamond accuracy on average over the four models, and 5.88 and 10.92 points on MMLU-Pro and Math-L5. NVFP4 reads with FP16+SR recurrence cut these losses to 2.36, 0.15, and 0.10 points, and with FP8+SR recurrence to 1.77, 0.40, and 0.38. Shared FP16 and FP8 checkpoints stay within the benchmark noise of FP32 even though their KL sits above the floor, so accuracy resolves only the larger KL gaps. Appendix E.4.6 gives the per-model table with output lengths. The loss concentrates in long generations, consistent with error that accumulates over a generation. GPQA-Diamond has the longest generations of the three benchmarks, and on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B its top reference-length quartile has a median of 61K tokens, against about 8K on MMLU-Pro and Math-L5. There, the gap between shared NVFP4+SR and FP32 grows from 0–2 points in the two shorter quartiles to 20.9 and 28.2 points in the two longer ones, while NVFP4 reads with FP8+SR recurrence keep the latter gaps at 2.0 and 3.4 points (Figure 6). Appendix E.4.7 repeats this for all models and benchmarks.

8 Related Work

Chunkwise SSM algorithms and prefix caching.

Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023) makes the SSM recurrence input dependent and keeps linear complexity with a hardware-aware parallel scan. Mamba-2 (Dao & Gu, 2024) restricts the decay to a scalar per head and, through structured state-space duality, organizes chunkwise computation around matrix multiplications. GDN (Yang et al., 2025) combines that decay with the targeted updates of the delta rule (Schlag et al., 2021), and KDA (Kimi Team, 2025) makes the decay channelwise. These recurrences keep chunkwise parallelism through the WY representation (Bischof & Van Loan, 1987) and the UT transform (Joffrain et al., 2006), following the DeltaNet algorithm of Yang et al. (2024). All of this work optimizes compute throughput in training and prefill. ReplaySSM targets memory-bound autoregressive decoding instead and separates output computation from checkpoint updates, so that the state is written only at flushes. Because non-flush steps compute outputs directly from the checkpoint and the cached recent inputs, they can reuse these chunkwise algorithms, with the buffered inputs followed by the current token, or by the tokens to verify, as the chunk. Marconi (Pan et al., 2025) adds prefix caching for hybrid models, with admission and eviction policies that weigh the reuse and storage cost of recurrent states. Prefix caching avoids repeated prefill computation and ReplaySSM reduces state traffic during decoding, so the two address different phases and can be used together.

SSM speculative decoding.

Attention handles rollback by moving the sequence pointer of the KV cache backward, and the rejected keys and values are never read again. An SSM cannot, since once the draft tokens have been eagerly summarized into the state, recovering the previous state is expensive. Serving systems such as vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) therefore work around this by storing a snapshot of the state after every verified token and selecting the one that matches the accepted prefix. This costs one read and TT writes per step against the one read and one write of standard decoding, and the TT snapshots per request cap the concurrency that GPU memory allows. Prior work avoids the per-token snapshots but still pays extra state traffic to recover the accepted state, and at a serving batch size none of it is more than a few percent faster than the snapshots (Appendix A). The Mamba in the Llama (Wang et al., 2024a) fuses recovery into the verification kernel, which replays the committed tokens from cached inputs onto a checkpoint and stores both the checkpoint and the end state, one read and two writes per step. Snakes and Ladders (Wu et al., 2024) re-runs the state update on the accepted prefix in one of two ways. Activation Replay does so in a separate launch from cached inputs. Joint Attainment appends a padded backtracking sequence to the next verification, whose variable length also requires one captured CUDA graph per possible acceptance outcome. Both schemes copy between a checkpoint and a working state, three reads and three or four writes per step. STree (Wu et al., 2026) extends the replay to tree-structured drafts. Each step first replays the accepted tokens in place on the checkpoint, one read and one write, then verifies the drafts with a masked tree scan that reads that state and writes nothing, two reads and one write per step. This overhead means that speculative decoding, a reliable speedup for Transformers, barely helps SSMs at serving batch sizes (Figure 4), creating a major disadvantage.

ReplaySSM also caches inputs rather than states, but it does not use the cache to recover a state after verification. The checkpoint plus the buffer of recent inputs is the state representation itself, in standard as well as speculative decoding, and it separates output computation from checkpoint updates. The checkpoint together with any prefix of the buffer is the state after that many accepted tokens, so recovery never re-runs a recurrence. Rollback moves a buffer pointer, verification reads the checkpoint once and computes the outputs from the buffer without materializing a state, and the checkpoint is written only at a flush, once per window of LL committed tokens. Most steps therefore read the state once and write nothing. Appendix A compares the state traffic and kernel latency of all methods on one layer shape.

SSM state quantization.

Q-Mamba (Tianqi et al., 2025) quantizes Mamba weights, activations, and the recurrent state after training. For the state it proposes Decoupled Scale Quantization, separate scales along the state and channel dimensions that absorb outliers in the state, and Efficient Selectivity Reconstruction, which fine-tunes about two percent of the parameters on calibration data. Its error analysis includes the term that carries the previous step’s rounding error through the decay, but its training simulation drops that term as small, and at inference the quantized state still feeds the next update. Its evaluation stops at 2048 tokens. The Nemotron 3 Ultra report (NVIDIA, 2026), to which authors of this paper contributed, quantizes the Mamba state cache to FP16 or 8-bit with stochastic rounding and explores periodic cache checkpointing, which stores and quantizes the state only every C​CCC steps and replays cached input activations to advance it in between. This is the first benefit of ReplaySSM (Section 6), fewer quantization events per token, and the report finds the same round-to-nearest bias that Appendix E.4.5 measures. It keeps one quantized state that both produces the outputs and feeds the next update, so rounding error still enters the recurrence, only less often. ReplaySSM removes the term from the recurrence. The separation of output computation from the checkpoint update lets the two roles use different precisions, so the high-precision checkpoint carries the recurrence while the low-precision copy is read only for outputs. What remains is the rounding of the read copy in each output, which Section 7.4 measures out to 128K tokens. The decoupled scales of Q-Mamba could further reduce that remaining read error, and they apply to either checkpoint.

9 Conclusion and Future Work

Conventional SSM decoding reads and writes the state at every step, fusing output computation with the state update. ReplaySSM unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint plus a buffer of recent inputs, which separates output computation from checkpoint updates. Most steps compute outputs and write no state, and the checkpoint is written once per window. This separation roughly halves the dominant state traffic, turns speculative rollback into a buffer-pointer move with output-only verification, and keeps a low-precision read checkpoint out of the recurrence, so its rounding error does not accumulate with generation length. In vLLM at serving batch sizes, where the conventional kernel is memory-bound, ReplaySSM speeds up standard decoding by 1.201.20–1.47×1.47\times and gives about 1.8×1.8\times the throughput of vLLM’s speculative decoding on two 120B-class models, and separate precisions reduce the output KL of an NVFP4 checkpoint by 1313–36×36\times at the longest measured generation length. ReplaySSM is adopted in large-scale production models and integrated into LLM serving systems (Appendix G).

Every step still reads the checkpoint, and that read is the next target. The checkpoint enters each step scaled by a per-head cumulative decay, so a head whose decay has become negligible can skip the read on non-flush steps and turn its flush into a pure write. Appendix F outlines this direction.

Appendix A Speculative decoding compared with prior methods

This appendix compares the kernel-level cost of ReplaySSM verification with four prior ways of handling the SSM state during verification. These are vLLM’s per-token snapshots, The Mamba in the Llama (Wang et al., 2024a), the two variants of Snakes and Ladders (Wu et al., 2024), and STree (Wu et al., 2026). Every method runs on one B300 at the Mamba-2 layer shape of Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B with an FP32 state, batched over B=256B=256 requests with one draft chain per request. One state, one request in one layer, is 4.24.2 MB, so the batch holds 1.071.07 GB of state per layer. TT counts the tokens processed per verification step and aa the committed tokens. Tree drafting is outside this comparison, so STree runs with a single chain and its tree mask reduces to a causal mask.

The prior kernels come from the authors’ repositories, STree at commit b9a0c2411 1 https://github.com/wyc1997/stree and The Mamba in the Llama at commit b702a3e22 2 https://github.com/itsdaniele/speculative_mamba, with only the changes needed to run them at this shape under the current Triton. Snakes and Ladders has no repository of its own. The STree repository, which shares its first author, implements both variants, and we use that implementation. For each method we time the kernel launches its implementation issues in one verification step.

All baselines are tuned. Both prior repositories hard-code one launch configuration and vLLM’s kernel picks its own from a heuristic, so we sweep the launch configuration of every kernel and report each at its best.33 3 At T=4T=4 and B=256B=256, tuning lowers the per-step kernel latency of STree from 18561856 to 10851085 μ\mus, The Mamba in the Llama from 22612261 to 923923, Snakes and Ladders from 29552955 to 14171417 (Activation Replay) and from 48984898 to 23042304 (Joint Attainment), and vLLM’s kernel from 10431043 to 831831. Across T=2T=2 to 88 the gain is 1.41.4–3.0×3.0\times for the prior kernels and 1.21.2–1.4×1.4\times for vLLM’s. STree’s released path takes 20792079 μ\mus at T=4T=4 against 10851085 for its algorithm. STree is also measured as its algorithm, the masked replay plus a read-only tree scan, rather than as its released path, which adds two state copies that are identities for one chain and would make it 1.71.7–2.1×2.1\times slower. It runs with a chunk size of 16 instead of its default of 256, which would pad the TT-token window to 256 positions.

A.1 Per-step operations and state traffic

R and W denote one full read and one full write of the state.

  • •

    vLLM. One launch. The kernel loads the state once and stores the state after each of the TT tokens to that token’s slot, so the accepted token’s snapshot is the next state and no recovery pass is needed. 1​R+T​W1\mathrm{R}+T\mathrm{W}, independent of acceptance.

  • •

    The Mamba in the Llama. One fused launch. It loads the checkpoint, or the end state when every draft was accepted, replays the tokens committed by the previous step from cached inputs, stores the new checkpoint, runs the TT current tokens, and stores the end state. 1​R+2​W1\mathrm{R}+2\mathrm{W} at every acceptance, since the checkpoint store is issued even when the replay is skipped, and a serial chain of up to 2​T−12T-1 steps.

  • •

    Snakes and Ladders, Activation Replay. Three launches. A multi-step scan re-runs the committed tokens in place on the checkpoint, the checkpoint is copied to a working buffer, and the same kernel verifies in place on that buffer. Each use of the kernel loads and stores the state, so 3​R+3​W3\mathrm{R}+3\mathrm{W}. The masked replay always runs TT steps, so the cost does not depend on acceptance. This path is the STree paper’s “Vanilla SD” baseline.

  • •

    Snakes and Ladders, Joint Attainment. The same kernel without an activation cache. Each request contributes two rows to one launch, a padded backtracking row that re-processes the committed tokens and a draft row that continues into the drafts, both starting from the state verified two steps earlier. A gather then copies the backtracking row’s state into both rows. 3​R+4​W3\mathrm{R}+4\mathrm{W}, and 2​T−12T-1 serial steps once the batch is padded to one length.

  • •

    STree. Two launches. The masked replay runs in place on the checkpoint, then a chunk-scan kernel verifies the drafts, reading the state as its initial state and storing none. 2​R+1​W2\mathrm{R}+1\mathrm{W}, independent of acceptance. The released path adds a beam-select self-copy and a checkpoint-to-working copy, 5​R+4​W5\mathrm{R}+4\mathrm{W} in total.

  • •

    ReplaySSM. A non-flush step reads the checkpoint once and computes the outputs from it and the input buffer (1​R1\mathrm{R}). A flush step, once per about L/aL/a steps, also writes the new checkpoint (1​R+1​W1\mathrm{R}+1\mathrm{W}).

Table 3 sets these counts against the bytes Nsight measures for one step.

A.2 Results

Figure 7 adds STree and The Mamba in the Llama to Figure 4. Neither beats vLLM’s snapshots at this batch size. STree costs 1.81×1.81\times the vLLM kernel at T=2T=2 and 1.00×1.00\times at T=8T=8, and The Mamba in the Llama is below it by about 6%6\% only at its cheapest acceptance for T≥6T\geq 6. Both variants of Snakes and Ladders are slower still, 1.41.4–2.2×2.2\times the vLLM kernel for Activation Replay and 2.72.7–3.2×3.2\times for Joint Attainment, so they are left out of the figure. Joint Attainment is the faster of the two at batch size one in its paper, but here the second row per request doubles the state bytes of the verify launch and lengthens its serial chain. ReplaySSM is 3.33.3–3.9×3.9\times faster than STree and 2.52.5–3.6×3.6\times faster than The Mamba in the Llama when every token is committed, and 3.53.5–5.3×5.3\times and 2.32.3–5.1×5.1\times with one token committed.

The prior papers report their speedups at small batch sizes against conventional standard decoding. At small batch the decode step is dominated by loading the model weights, and verifying TT tokens per step amortizes that load over several tokens. This gain belongs to speculative decoding itself and does not depend on how the SSM state is handled. At a serving batch size the weights are already amortized and the state traffic is the bottleneck (Section 3.1), so the cost of state recovery decides whether speculation pays off, and there none of the prior methods pays off against vLLM’s snapshots.

Table 3 also shows that fewer bytes do not buy these methods lower latency. At T≥4T\geq 4 STree and The Mamba in the Llama move 1.61.6–2.9×2.9\times fewer state bytes than vLLM’s kernel, yet they are not faster. Their recovery kernels are serial recurrences that hold the state tile in registers for TT or 2​T−12T-1 steps, which limits occupancy and leaves most of the DRAM bandwidth idle, more so as TT grows.

Appendix B GDN derivations and algorithms

B.1 Outer-product and unrolled forms

We derive Equation 3 from Equation 2 and unroll it over a replay window, the form the GDN algorithms in this appendix use.

Outer-product form.

Distributing the product in Equation 2 gives

St\displaystyle S_{t} =αt​St−1​(I−βt​kt​kt⊤)+βt​vt​kt⊤\displaystyle=\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}\left(I-\beta_{t}k_{t}k_{t}^{\top}\right)+\beta_{t}v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}
=αt​St−1−αt​βt​(St−1​kt)​kt⊤+βt​vt​kt⊤\displaystyle=\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}-\alpha_{t}\beta_{t}\left(S_{t-1}k_{t}\right)k_{t}^{\top}+\beta_{t}v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}

B.2 Standard decoding

Algorithm 4 is the GDN counterpart of Algorithm 4. The two differ in the order of the first steps. Mamba-2 appends the record and then reconstructs the state, because vtv_{t} is known before the step. GDN reconstructs St−1S_{t-1} first (Line 1), since the correction in Line 2 needs St−1​ktS_{t-1}k_{t}, and only then appends (αt,ut,kt)(\alpha_{t},u_{t},k_{t}) and advances the state (Lines 3–4). By Equation 8, Line 4 equals Replay(Sckpt,ℬ1:h)\textsc{Replay}(S_{\mathrm{ckpt}},\mathcal{B}_{1:h}) over the updated buffer, so the flush branch is unchanged.

The correction utu_{t} is computed in FP32 from the reconstructed state. With BF16 activations we cache it in FP16 rather than BF16, since FP16 keeps 10 mantissa bits of that result against 7 for BF16 at the same storage cost.

B.3 Speculative decoding

GDN verifies drafts with the output-only evaluation of Section 5.2 and keeps the buffer handling of Algorithm 4: draft records are written behind the committed ones and the accepted prefix is committed by moving hh. The difficulty is that a draft’s correction depends on the state just before it (Equation 3), which includes the effect of the earlier drafts in the window. Output-only verification still applies: the TT draft corrections follow from one T×TT\times T triangular solve, after which Equation 6 applies with corrections in place of values. Algorithm 5 assembles the step.

Let draft ss sit at window position t=h+st=h+s. Equation 8 at t−1t-1 gives

αtSt−1kt=γtSckptkt+∑j=1t−1γj+1:t(kj⊤kt)uj.\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}k_{t}=\gamma_{t}S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}k_{t}+\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\gamma_{j+1:t}\,(k_{j}^{\top}k_{t})\,u_{j}. (9)

The terms with j≤hj\leq h use cached corrections; those with h<j<th<j<t involve earlier drafts, whose corrections are unknown. where Aj​s=γh+j+1:h+skh+j⊤kh+sA_{js}=\gamma_{h+j+1:h+s}\,k_{h+j}^{\top}k_{h+s} for j<sj<s and 00 otherwise, DD is the diagonal decay matrix of Equation 6, and Wc∈ℝh×TW_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times T} is the first hh rows of the (h+T)×T(h+T)\times T matrix WW of Equation 6. The known part RR has the shape of Equation 6 with the draft keys in place of the queries. I+A​BdI+AB_{d} is unit upper triangular, so one T×TT\times T triangular solve yields UdU_{d}; this is the UT transform used to parallelize delta-rule training (Yang et al., 2024). With U=[Uc,Ud]U=[U_{c},U_{d}], the outputs are Equation 6 with UU in place of VV:

O=Sckpt​Q​D+U⁡(W⊙(K⊤​Q)).O=S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}QD+U\bigl(W\odot(K^{\top}Q)\bigr). (11)

SckptS_{\mathrm{ckpt}} enters only through Sckpt​KdS_{\mathrm{ckpt}}K_{d} and Sckpt​QS_{\mathrm{ckpt}}Q, which one pass over the checkpoint computes together.

Algorithm 5 differs from Algorithm 4 only in its first three lines. The draft records hold corrections rather than values, so they can be appended only after Equation 10 is solved (Lines 2–3), which in turn needs the checkpoint loaded first (Line 1). Line 4 is Equation 11. Flush, acceptance, and commit are unchanged: each accepted correction depends only on the checkpoint and the records before it, so it remains a valid record, and the flush replays committed records only. In our kernel, Lines 2, 4, and 6 share one pass over the checkpoint.

B.4 Low-precision state

Algorithm 4 keeps low-precision error out of the recurrence because Mamba-2 records hold raw inputs: a flush replays (α,v,k)(\alpha,v,k) records from the high-precision checkpoint, and nothing read from the low-precision copy is written back. GDN records hold corrections, and each correction is computed from the state its step read (Equation 3). On non-flush steps that state comes from the low-precision checkpoint, so the cached uju_{j} carry its rounding error. If a flush folds these corrections into the high-precision checkpoint, the error enters the recurrence, and each flush cycle adds its own: the checkpoint error becomes a sum over all past cycles, finite for any decay below one but growing without bound as the decay approaches one. Folding cached corrections is therefore stable only under a data-dependent condition.

We avoid this by caching the raw inputs as well. In the two-precision variant a GDN record holds (α,β,u,v,k)(\alpha,\beta,u,v,k). Non-flush steps use uu as before. A flush ignores the cached corrections and re-derives them from the high-precision checkpoint along Equation 8, uj=βj​(vj−αj​Sj−1​kj)u_{j}=\beta_{j}(v_{j}-\alpha_{j}S_{j-1}k_{j}) with Sj−1S_{j-1} on the high-precision path. The low-precision copy then never enters the recurrence, and the high-precision path is exact up to its own rounding, as for Mamba-2. The two flush paths differ only when the read checkpoint is low precision. A cached correction carries the rounding of the state it was computed from, so folding it writes that error into the checkpoint, where every later window inherits it. Re-deriving it from the high-precision checkpoint and the cached raw inputs folds a clean value, so the error stays in the outputs computed before the flush. With an FP32 checkpoint the sole difference is that a cached correction is stored in the FP16 record format while a re-derived one is formed in FP32 on the fly. Our FP32 speedup measurements therefore fold the cached corrections, and all low-precision results re-derive them.

Algorithm 6 extends Algorithm 5 the way Algorithm 4 extends Algorithm 4. The changes, shown in color, are the precision choice and load (Lines 1–2), the extended record (Line 4), the re-derivation at flush (Line 7), and the two casts and stores (Lines 8–9). Acceptance, rollback, and buffer management are unchanged.

Appendix C Cost and numerical error analysis

C.1 Arithmetic intensity of conventional decoding

Taking Mamba-2 as the example, we count the bytes moved and the FLOPs performed by one head in one conventional decoding step (Equation 1). The state St∈ℝdv×dkS_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{k}} is stored with bb bytes per element (b=4b=4 for FP32, b=2b=2 for FP16 or BF16).

Memory traffic.

The step loads St−1S_{t-1} and stores StS_{t}, moving 2​b​dv​dk2b\,d_{v}d_{k} bytes. It also reads αt\alpha_{t}, vtv_{t}, ktk_{t}, and qtq_{t} and writes oto_{t}, but these are vectors of length dvd_{v} or dkd_{k}, negligible against the dv​dkd_{v}d_{k} state.

FLOPs.

A multiplication and an addition count as two FLOPs. The decay αt​St−1\alpha_{t}S_{t-1}, the outer product vt​kt⊤v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}, their sum, and the readout St​qtS_{t}q_{t} cost dv​dkd_{v}d_{k}, dv​dkd_{v}d_{k}, dv​dkd_{v}d_{k}, and 2​dv​dk−dv2d_{v}d_{k}-d_{v} FLOPs, so the step performs 5​dv​dk−dv5d_{v}d_{k}-d_{v} FLOPs.

Arithmetic intensity.

The ratio of FLOPs to bytes is

Iconv=5​dv​dk−dv2​b​dv​dk≈52​b​FLOP per byte,I_{\mathrm{conv}}=\frac{5d_{v}d_{k}-d_{v}}{2b\,d_{v}d_{k}}\approx\frac{5}{2b}\;\text{FLOP per byte}, (12)

about 0.630.63 for an FP32 state and 1.251.25 for FP16. Batching does not raise it, because every sequence brings its own state and no state element is reused, so traffic and FLOPs scale together. An H100 needs about 2020 FLOP per byte of HBM traffic to keep its FP32 CUDA cores busy, and about 300300 for its BF16 tensor cores (NVIDIA Corporation, 2022). Conventional SSM decoding runs at under 11, so the step is bottlenecked by moving the state through HBM, not by arithmetic.

C.2 SSM and attention traffic in a hybrid model

Section 3.1 states that the SSM layers of Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4 move more bytes per decoding step than its attention layers until the context reaches about 80K tokens. We count the bytes here from the shapes in the released model configuration.44 4 https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4/blob/main/config.json Table 5 lists the SSM shapes.

State size.

Each Mamba-2 layer has 128 value heads with dv=64d_{v}=64 and dk=128d_{k}=128 and stores its state in FP32, so the state is 128×64×128×4128\times 64\times 128\times 4 bytes, or 4 MiB per sequence. A decoding step loads and stores it, moving 8 MiB per sequence per layer.

KV cache size.

Each attention layer has 2 key-value heads of dimension 128 and stores keys and values in FP8, so one token’s entry is 2×2×1282\times 2\times 128 bytes, or 0.5 KiB. One SSM state therefore equals the KV cache for 4​MiB/0.5​KiB=81924~\mathrm{MiB}/0.5~\mathrm{KiB}=8192 tokens. A decoding step at context length NN loads the NN entries, about 0.5​N0.5N KiB per sequence per layer.

Crossover.

With 40 Mamba-2 layers and 8 attention layers, the SSM layers move 40×8=32040\times 8=320 MiB per sequence per step and the attention layers move 8×0.5​N=4​N8\times 0.5N=4N KiB. The totals are equal at N=81,920N=81{,}920 tokens, the layer ratio of five times 8K tokens times two for the load and the store. Batching does not move the crossover, since both totals scale with the number of sequences. The measured crossover in Figure 1 (bottom left) comes later, near 100K tokens, which is consistent with attention kernels having received more optimization effort (Dao et al., 2022, e.g.,).

C.3 Memory traffic

We compare the HBM traffic of conventional decoding and ReplaySSM standard decoding (Algorithm 4) for one Mamba-2 head over one replay window of LL steps, with an FP32 state, BF16 values and keys, and an FP32 decay. The window has L−1L-1 non-flush steps and one flush step. Both methods read the current token’s αt\alpha_{t}, vtv_{t}, ktk_{t}, and qtq_{t} and write oto_{t} at every step; this traffic is identical on both sides and negligible (Appendix C.1), so we omit it from both totals. The buffer traffic that ReplaySSM adds is counted.

Traffic per window.

Conventional decoding loads and stores the 4​dv​dk4d_{v}d_{k}-byte state at every step, so one window moves 8​L​dv​dk8L\,d_{v}d_{k} bytes. ReplaySSM loads the checkpoint at every step and stores it once, at the flush, 4​(L+1)​dv​dk4(L+1)\,d_{v}d_{k} bytes, and adds the buffer traffic. A record holds vjv_{j} and kjk_{j} in BF16 and αj\alpha_{j} in FP32, r=2​dv+2​dk+4r=2d_{v}+2d_{k}+4 bytes. The ii-th non-flush step, i=1,…,L−1i=1,\ldots,L-1, loads the i−1i-1 buffered records and stores the current input as one record; the flush step loads all L−1L-1 records and folds the current input into the checkpoint directly, storing no record. Over the window, reads total ∑i=1L−1(i−1)+(L−1)=L⁡(L−1)/2\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}(i-1)+(L-1)=L(L-1)/2 records and writes total L−1L-1, so (L−1)​(L+2)/2(L-1)(L+2)/2 record transfers in all. The two totals are

Mconv=8​L​dv​dk,Mreplay=4​(L+1)​dv​dk+(L−1)​(L+2)2​r.M_{\mathrm{conv}}=8L\,d_{v}d_{k},\qquad M_{\mathrm{replay}}=4(L+1)\,d_{v}d_{k}+\frac{(L-1)(L+2)}{2}\,r. (13)

The checkpoint term alone gives the ratio (L+1)/(2​L)(L+1)/(2L), just above one half for any LL; the buffer term grows quadratically in LL and sets the window-size tradeoff of Appendix C.5.

Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B.

Its Mamba-2 layers have dv=64d_{v}=64 and dk=128d_{k}=128. With L=16L=16, Equation 13 gives Mreplay/Mconv=0.58M_{\mathrm{replay}}/M_{\mathrm{conv}}=0.58, a 1.7×1.7\times reduction in memory traffic. The figure is conservative. Mamba-2 shares each key across the 1616 heads of a group, so the per-head key traffic is smaller than the record size counts.

Speculative decoding.

Table 3 in Appendix A extends this count to verification steps and compares it with vLLM’s snapshots and the prior recovery methods, as read and write counts and as Nsight bytes.

C.4 FLOPs for output-only computation

Section 5.2 introduced output-only evaluation, which computes o=v⁡(k⊤​q)o=v(k^{\top}q) without materializing the state. Because kk and qq are shared by the heads of a group, k⊤​qk^{\top}q is also computed once per group rather than once per head. Here we count the FLOPs.

FLOPs do not set the latency of a memory-bound kernel in standard decoding with an FP32 state (Appendix C.1), but they matter as arithmetic intensity rises. A lower-precision state moves fewer bytes per step, and speculative decoding multiplies the arithmetic per step by the number of tokens verified. Not materializing the state also saves on-chip memory. We count per head with the rule of Appendix C.1 and keep only the leading term of each count in dvd_{v} and dkd_{k}.

Standard decoding.

Algorithm 4 materializes the state before the readout, and the main text presents only that route for standard decoding. Output-only evaluation applies there as well, so we count both routes. With hh buffered records and the current input, a step applies h+1h+1 value-key pairs. The state-and-output route (Algorithm 4) costs

  • •

    decayed checkpoint plus h+1h+1 weighted outer products, summed: 2​(h+2)​dv​dk2(h+2)\,d_{v}d_{k};

  • •

    readout St​qtS_{t}q_{t}: 2​dv​dk2d_{v}d_{k};

The term that materializes the state, 2​(h+1)​dv​dk2(h+1)\,d_{v}d_{k}, becomes 2​(h+1)​(dv+dk)2(h+1)(d_{v}+d_{k}), smaller by a factor dv​dk/(dv+dk)d_{v}d_{k}/(d_{v}+d_{k}), about 4343 for the shapes of Appendix C.3.

C.5 Replay-window tradeoff

A larger window amortizes each checkpoint write over more tokens but makes every step load more records. We extend the traffic analysis of Appendix C.3 to speculative decoding and solve for the window that minimizes traffic per committed token, treating the kernel as purely memory-bound. In practice the FLOPs and on-chip buffer storage of Appendix C.4 also enter, so the result is an approximation. Let MS=4​dv​dkM_{S}=4d_{v}d_{k} be the state size in bytes, rr the record size, TT the tokens per step, and a¯\bar{a} the mean number of tokens committed per step. One flush cycle commits LL tokens over L/a¯L/\bar{a} steps and moves

  • •

    checkpoint reads, one per step: MS​L/a¯M_{S}\,L/\bar{a};

  • •

    checkpoint write, one per cycle: MSM_{S};

  • •

    buffer reads: at the ii-th step of the cycle the buffer holds i​a¯i\bar{a} committed records, i=0,…,L/a¯−1i=0,\ldots,L/\bar{a}-1, so r​a¯​∑ii=r​L​(L−a¯)/(2​a¯)r\bar{a}\sum_{i}i=rL(L-\bar{a})/(2\bar{a});

  • •

    buffer writes: TT records per step, written before verification so rejected drafts are paid for too, and none at the flush step: r​T​(L/a¯−1)rT(L/\bar{a}-1).

Dividing by LL gives the traffic per committed token,

f⁡(L)=MSa¯+MSL+r​L2​a¯−r2+r​Ta¯−r​TL,f(L)=\frac{M_{S}}{\bar{a}}+\frac{M_{S}}{L}+\frac{rL}{2\bar{a}}-\frac{r}{2}+\frac{rT}{\bar{a}}-\frac{rT}{L}, (15)

which for a¯=T=1\bar{a}=T=1 equals Mreplay/LM_{\mathrm{replay}}/L of Equation 13. Setting f′​(L)=0f^{\prime}(L)=0 gives

L∗=2​a¯​(MSr−T).L^{*}=\sqrt{2\bar{a}\left(\frac{M_{S}}{r}-T\right)}. (16)

The optimum grows with the state-to-record size ratio and with the square root of the acceptance rate, since higher acceptance commits more tokens per checkpoint read. The model also treats a cycle as exactly L/a¯L/\bar{a} steps. The flush fires when h+T>Lh+T>L, so a cycle commits between L−T+1L-T+1 and LL tokens depending on where the last acceptance lands, and flushes come somewhat more often than the model assumes.

With the shapes of Appendix C.3, MS/r=84M_{S}/r=84.
