C.6 Quantization error propagation

Rounding modes.

Storing the state in a low-precision format rounds each element to one of its two representable neighbours, which lie a distance δ\delta apart that depends on the element’s magnitude. Round-to-nearest (RTN) picks the closer one. Its error is at most δ/2\delta/2, but its sign depends on the value, so the errors of similar values share a direction and add up. Stochastic rounding (SR) uses the position of the value within the gap. If the value lies a fraction pp of the way from the lower neighbour to the upper one, SR rounds up with probability pp and down with probability 1−p1-p, so the rounded value equals the original in expectation. SR removes the bias but not the error. Each rounding is a zero-mean error with variance p⁡(1−p)​δ2p(1-p)\delta^{2}, at most δ2/4\delta^{2}/4. The analysis below models these two behaviours as a per-element bias bb and variance σ2\sigma^{2}.

Propagation through the recurrence.

Let StS_{t} follow Equation 1 exactly, and let S^t\hat{S}_{t} be the stored state, which is rounded by 𝒬\mathcal{Q} after every update: S^t=𝒬⁡(Xt)\hat{S}_{t}=\mathcal{Q}(X_{t}) with Xt=αt​S^t−1+vt​kt⊤X_{t}=\alpha_{t}\hat{S}_{t-1}+v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}. The rounding error of step tt is et=𝒬⁡(Xt)−Xte_{t}=\mathcal{Q}(X_{t})-X_{t}, and the accumulated deviation of the stored state from the exact one is Dt=S^t−StD_{t}=\hat{S}_{t}-S_{t}. Subtracting the two recurrences gives

Dt=αtDt−1+et=∑j≤tγj+1:tej,D_{t}=\alpha_{t}D_{t-1}+e_{t}=\sum_{j\leq t}\gamma_{j+1:t}\,e_{j}, (17)

so each step’s rounding error is decayed by later steps but never removed, and the output error is Dt​qtD_{t}q_{t}. To see the scaling, take a constant decay α\alpha and errors that are independent across steps with bias bb and variance σ2\sigma^{2} per element. The mean deviation converges to b/(1−α)b/(1-\alpha) and the variance to σ2/(1−α2)\sigma^{2}/(1-\alpha^{2}), both reached after a number of steps on the order of 1/(1−α)1/(1-\alpha). RTN contributes through the first term and SR only through the second. Both limits are finite for α<1\alpha<1 and grow without bound as α→1\alpha\to 1. Since α\alpha is a per-head, data-dependent quantity, the saturation level is head dependent. Heads with slow decay, which hold information over long horizons, accumulate the most error under this analysis.

Effect of ReplaySSM.

With a single low-precision checkpoint, rounding occurs once per window rather than once per step, and the deviation decays by γL=αL\gamma_{L}=\alpha^{L} between injections. The limits become b/(1−αL)b/(1-\alpha^{L}) and σ2/(1−α2​L)\sigma^{2}/(1-\alpha^{2L}), lower than the conventional ones because αL<α\alpha^{L}<\alpha, but still growing as α→1\alpha\to 1. With separate precisions, the recurrence runs on the high-precision checkpoint and the low-precision copy is read only for outputs, so its rounding error never enters Equation 17. The output error at a non-flush step is a single rounding, independent of α\alpha and of the sequence length.

Limits of the analysis.

The analysis predicts how error scales with decay and window size, not its magnitude. It assumes independent errors with fixed bias and variance, whereas real rounding errors depend on the values being rounded and can partly cancel. We therefore measure the error directly as the KL divergence between the next-token distributions of low-precision and FP32-state decoding; Appendix E.4.3 defines the measurement and Section 7.4 reports it.

Appendix D Serving implementation

We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and GDN, but nothing in the design depends on vLLM. The released source code records the buffer layout, its placement in the paged state, and the cursor bookkeeping. This appendix covers the two decisions that determine how the kernels behave inside a serving engine, the flush rule under speculative decoding and execution under CUDA graphs.

D.1 Flush rule under speculative decoding

In standard decoding the buffer holds LL records, each token is committed when it is appended, and the flush fires when the buffer is full (Algorithm 4). Speculative decoding appends TT records per step and commits only aa of them, and aa is known only after the step, so the rule changes. The ring has capacity L+TL+T, and we keep the invariant that at most LL committed records are in the buffer at the start of a step, so the TT records of the step always fit behind them. Suppose a step with hh committed records does not flush and all TT tokens are accepted. The committed length becomes h+Th+T, and the next step appends TT more records at positions up to h+2​Th+2T. When h+T>Lh+T>L this exceeds the capacity L+TL+T, and in a ring the new records overwrite committed ones. Algorithm 4 therefore flushes exactly when h+T>Lh+T>L. The flush folds the hh committed records into the checkpoint before acceptance is known, which is valid because they stay committed whatever the verifier returns, and the committed length after the step is a≤T≤La\leq T\leq L, so the invariant holds.

The rule depends only on hh and TT, both known before the step runs, so the decision never waits on sampling. It is an early flush in the sense that it may fire when a partial acceptance would have left room. The flush interval is therefore not fixed at LL steps as in standard decoding but roughly L/aL/a steps, and higher acceptance flushes more often. This is the band in Figures 4 and 10.

D.2 CUDA graphs

Serving engines capture the decode step as a CUDA graph and replay it, which removes the CPU launch overhead of the many small kernels in a step. A captured graph fixes the launch sequence for a batch size, so any decision that varies within a batch has to be made on the device. ReplaySSM needs two such decisions.

The first is whether a row flushes. Under continuous batching the rows of a batch were admitted at different times and sit at different buffer positions, so they reach their flush steps at different times. Speculative decoding adds a second source of divergence, because each row commits its own aa. At a given step some rows flush and others do not, and one graph has to serve them all. ReplaySSM therefore treats the flush decision as per-row data that the kernels read at run time rather than a compile-time constant. The flush work is either a branch inside the decode kernel or a separate launch specialized for flushing, from which non-flushing rows exit at once. Either way one captured graph per batch size covers both kinds of rows, and the inactive rows of a padded batch exit the same way.

The second is the commit after verification. The accepted count aa is known only after sampling and differs across rows. Reading it back to the host would add a device-to-host synchronization at every step and stall the pipeline. Instead a small commit kernel runs on the device. It advances each row’s buffer pointer by that row’s aa, moves the ring origin past the flushed records on a flush step, and sets the flush flags of the next step, since the rule of Appendix D.1 depends only on the resulting hh and on TT. Every cursor update stays inside the captured work.

Appendix E Additional evaluation details and results

E.1 Evaluation setup

Models.

Table 5 adds the layer counts and the SSM-layer shape of each model to Table 1; the kernel benchmarks in this appendix run at these shapes. Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B and both Qwen3.5 models ship a multi-token-prediction (MTP) head; the speculative-decoding experiments use it as the drafter on the two 120B-class models. Throughout the paper, “FP32 state” refers to the SSM state only; weights keep their released precision (Table 1) and activations are BF16. FP32 is also the SSM state precision all four models default to in vLLM. The Qwen3.5 models set mamba_ssm_dtype and Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B sets mamba_ssm_cache_dtype to float32 in their released configurations, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B leaves it unset, so vLLM applies its float32 default for NemotronH models.55 5 Configuration files of https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B, https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4, and https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4; the NemotronH default is set in vllm/model_executor/models/config.py of the vLLM repository.

Hardware and software.

The 4B models run on one H100 with 80 GB of HBM3, and the 120B-class models on one B300 under a 1100 W power cap, all without tensor parallelism. The performance experiments run the ReplaySSM kernels inside vLLM against vLLM’s own kernels, both in the same build with CUDA graphs enabled. The low-precision experiments use emulated quantization. The KL and accuracy measurements run a Triton kernel that implements Algorithm 4 with quantized checkpoints inside the same vLLM integration, and the low-precision latency measurements (Appendix E.4.2) use separate CuTe DSL kernels.

Measurement protocol.

Unless a figure states otherwise, performance measurements use an FP32 state, L=16L=16, and greedy decoding. Kernel latencies are standalone measurements at the model’s SSM shape, after warmup and with a cold L2, and each ReplaySSM measurement covers full replay windows. Conventional kernels are timed at the best launch configuration found by a sweep (Appendix E.2.1). Reported latencies are medians over repeated launches.

E.2 Standard decoding

E.2.1 Batch-size sweep

The baseline is vLLM’s kernel at the best launch configuration found by a sweep, not at its shipped default. vLLM picks its Mamba-2 configuration from a heuristic with no tuned entry for either shape we evaluate, while the shipped GDN configuration is already the swept optimum.66 6 Against the shipped Mamba-2 default, the speedups at B=256B=256 would read 1.49×1.49\times end-to-end and 1.89×1.89\times for the kernel on Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, and 1.48×1.48\times and 1.75×1.75\times on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B, instead of the 1.471.47/1.801.80 and 1.421.42/1.531.53 we report. ReplaySSM speeds up standard decoding at serving batch sizes, where the conventional kernel is memory-bound, and not at small batches, where it is not. Figure 8 sweeps the batch size on Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, and Tables 7 and 7 give the end-to-end and kernel speedups for all four models. At B=1B=1 the speedup is below parity (0.410.41–0.88×0.88\times for the kernel, 0.960.96–0.99×0.99\times for the decode step), because the conventional kernel reaches only 21.6%21.6\% of peak DRAM bandwidth on H100 and 9.3%9.3\% on B300, so reducing its memory traffic saves nothing. From B≈128B\approx 128 the baseline saturates at 8484–86%86\% of peak and the kernel speedup levels off at 1.41.4–1.8×1.8\times, while the end-to-end speedup keeps growing because the SSM layers take a larger share of the decode step as the batch grows. The end-to-end gain is also largest at short and medium sequence lengths; at long sequences attention dominates the step, since its KV-cache traffic grows linearly with sequence length (Figure 1, bottom left).

E.2.2 Replay-window sweep

The window size trades flush frequency against per-step work. A shorter window flushes more often and pays for more checkpoint writes; a longer window flushes less often, but every step reads more from the buffer. Figure 9 sweeps L∈{8,16,32}L\in\{8,16,32\} at B=256B=256. The amortized kernel latency is lowest at L=16L=16 for all four models. The traffic analysis of Appendix C.5 predicts an optimum near L=13L=13 for standard decoding, and L=16L=16 is the nearest power of two.

E.3 Speculative decoding

Both models draft with their MTP head. The acceptance length is the mean number of tokens committed per step. Requests are GSM8K prompts (Cobbe et al., 2021) served at a fixed batch size BB; every request generates 256 tokens with end-of-sequence ignored, and the timed window covers the whole request, prefill included, after warmup. Throughput is the total number of generated tokens divided by the wall time.

E.3.1 Serving throughput across batch size and verification length

Tables 9 and 9 give the throughput of ReplaySSM speculative decoding relative to conventional vLLM speculative decoding over the full grid of BB and TT, and Table 10 the acceptance lengths at B=256B=256. Three points hold on both models. At B=1B=1 the two methods are close (0.880.88–1.17×1.17\times on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4, 0.870.87–1.12×1.12\times on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4), because at small batch the state traffic that ReplaySSM removes is not the bottleneck. At larger batch the speedup grows with both BB and TT, and it has two sources. Conventional speculation stores one state snapshot per draft token, so its state traffic and storage grow with BB and TT together; the storage caps the concurrency that GPU memory allows, and its throughput saturates from B≈128B\approx 128 and at large TT falls below standard decoding.77 7 On Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4 at B=256B=256, conventional speculation peaks at T=2T=2 with 9,551 tokens/s and drops to 5,644 at T=8T=8, below standard decoding at 6,807. ReplaySSM writes the state only on flush steps and verifies with the faster kernel of Figure 4, so it keeps scaling. Acceptance lengths agree within 0.050.05 tokens in every cell (Table 10), so the gain does not come from a different acceptance behavior.

E.3.2 Kernel latency on GDN

Figure 10 repeats Figure 4 for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. GDN shows the same trend as Mamba-2. The conventional kernel costs 2.09×2.09\times a standard decoding step at T=2T=2 and 6.40×6.40\times at T=8T=8, while ReplaySSM stays at 0.830.83–0.95×0.95\times up to T=4T=4 and 1.111.11–1.33×1.33\times at T=8T=8, flushes included, with each band spanning a=1a=1 to a=Ta=T (Appendix D.1). The step between T=4T=4 and T=6T=6 comes from tiling. Some kernel internals pad the verification window to a multiple of four tokens, so T=6T=6 pays for eight.

E.4 Low-precision state

E.4.1 Formats and quantization

We store checkpoints in four formats. FP32 and FP16 are unscaled. FP8 uses E4M3 elements with one FP32 scale per block of 128 contiguous elements along the key dimension, which is one scale per state row since dk=128d_{k}=128 for all four models. NVFP4 uses E2M1 elements with one E4M3 scale per block of 16 elements and one FP32 scale per state. A flush accumulates the new checkpoint in FP32 from the recurrence checkpoint and the buffered inputs and casts that FP32 result into each stored copy independently, never one copy from another. The cast into the recurrence checkpoint uses stochastic rounding when that checkpoint is FP16 or FP8, and the cast into the read checkpoint uses round-to-nearest. A shared checkpoint is a single copy written with stochastic rounding; Appendix E.4.5 shows what happens when it is written with round-to-nearest instead. Quantization applies to decoding only. Prefill computes the state at full precision, and rounding enters only through checkpoint writes during generation. All low-precision results use L=16L=16 and standard decoding. Speculative decoding changes how many tokens a step verifies, and acceptance sets when flushes occur. Neither changes which values are rounded, so the error mechanism is the same.

E.4.2 Latency of low-precision reads

The point of the separate checkpoints in Section 6 is to keep rounding error out of the recurrence. A lower-precision read checkpoint also moves fewer bytes on every non-flush step, so it can lower latency as well, and Figure 11 quantifies that gain. It measures the non-flush kernel of standard decoding at B=256B=256 with CuTe DSL kernels, varying only the read checkpoint while the FP16+SR recurrence checkpoint, which a non-flush step never touches, stays fixed. Relative to an FP32 state, an FP16 read runs 1.61×1.61\times faster on Mamba-2 and 1.68×1.68\times on GDN, an FP8 read 2.82×2.82\times and 2.48×2.48\times, and an NVFP4 read 3.83×3.83\times and 2.76×2.76\times. These are non-flush ratios. Over a full window the gain is smaller, since flush steps still read and write the higher-precision checkpoint; on Mamba-2 at B=512B=512 the NVFP4 read gives 4.11×4.11\times on non-flush steps and 3.33×3.33\times over the window. Under speculative decoding it is smaller still, since flushes are more frequent and each step carries more arithmetic.

E.4.3 Output KL across models

Setting.

We decode four streams, each one book from the PG-19 test split (Rae et al., 2019), from a 512-token prompt under teacher forcing. At every step we record the model’s logits and replace the sampled token with the book’s next token, so all configurations consume the same token sequence and only the recurrent state differs. The metric is DKL(pFP32∥pconfig)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{FP32}}\|p_{\mathrm{config}}) over the full vocabulary, averaged over the four streams and the 256 positions ending at NN, where pFP32p_{\mathrm{FP32}} is conventional FP32-state decoding with CUDA graphs. One seed per configuration.

Results.

Figure 12 shows the three models not in Figure 6, and three points hold across all four. First, a shared low-precision checkpoint accumulates error with NN, while a separate recurrence removes most of the growth. At the last plotted NN, NVFP4 reads with FP32 recurrence sit 1313–29×29\times below a shared NVFP4 checkpoint (arrows in Figure 12), and FP16+SR recurrence tracks FP32 recurrence within 1.25×1.25\times at every point but one. The growth is reduced rather than removed, since on the two Nemotron models the curves with a separate recurrence still rise a few times over the range. Second, a lower read precision raises the starting point of a curve. On Nemotron-3-Nano-4B at N=16N=16, an FP8 read sits at 1.2×10−31.2\times 10^{-3} and an NVFP4 read at 2×10−22\times 10^{-2}, against a floor of 3.7×10−43.7\times 10^{-4}. Third, Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4 and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-NVFP4 have floors about two orders of magnitude above the 4B models, at 11–3×10−23\times 10^{-2}. They differ from the 4B models in size, weight precision, and expert routing at once, and our data do not attribute the floor to any one of these. Two conventional FP32 runs that differ only in execution path, eager against CUDA graph, are already this far apart on these models, so the floor is numerical noise rather than error that ReplaySSM introduces, and each configuration should be judged by its distance above the floor of its panel. Nemotron-3-Nano-4B is plotted only to 32K, because beyond that its FP32 reference becomes nearly one-hot on the end-of-turn token, which deflates every configuration’s KL.88 8 The mean probability of the end-of-turn token is 0.760.76 at 64K and 0.880.88 at 128K. The other three models place no measurable probability on that token at any NN.

E.4.4 Window-size sensitivity of KL

Figure 13 repeats the KL measurement on Qwen3.5-4B at L∈{1,4,16,32,64}L\in\{1,4,16,32,64\} for two shared and two separate configurations; the separate ones use FP32 recurrence here. L=1L=1 is conventional decoding, where the state is written and downcast at every step. It exists only for a shared checkpoint, since the separate configurations need the non-flush steps that a window of L>1L>1 creates.

The two kinds of configuration respond to LL in the two ways Section 6 describes. A shared checkpoint is requantized at every flush, so a longer window means fewer rounding events and a lower KL. From L=1L=1 to 6464 the number of checkpoint writes falls 64×64\times. Over the same range the KL of the shared FP8 checkpoint falls 12×12\times at N=1N=1K and 10×10\times at 128K, and that of the shared NVFP4 checkpoint falls 23×23\times and 4.8×4.8\times. The gain is less than proportional to the number of rounding events, as Appendix C.6 predicts. At the L=16L=16 we use, the shared FP8 and NVFP4 checkpoints sit 3.8×3.8\times and 2.6×2.6\times below conventional per-step quantization at 128K, which is the first benefit of ReplaySSM for a low-precision state. The separate configurations barely change across LL. They move by 1.11.1–1.2×1.2\times between L=4L=4 and 6464, the same as the scatter of the FP32-state floor itself (1.051.05–1.06×1.06\times). Their read checkpoint is regenerated from the unquantized recurrence at every flush and never fed back, so each output sees one rounding of a clean state however many flushes preceded it, and LL barely affects it.99 9 On GDN the corrections uu cached on non-flush steps are computed from the low-precision read checkpoint and enter the outputs of the rest of the window, which leaves a small dependence on LL. The flush re-derives them from the high-precision path (Appendix B.4), so this error does not reach the recurrence.

E.4.5 Stochastic rounding against round-to-nearest

Appendix E.4.1 writes the recurrence checkpoint with stochastic rounding and the read copy with round-to-nearest. Table 11 gives the reason. It compares the two rounding modes on a shared checkpoint at L=16L=16 through the ratio of the RTN KL to the SR KL at matched precision, which cancels the FP32 floor. At short generation lengths RTN is close to or below SR. At N=1N=1K it gives 0.400.40–0.51×0.51\times the SR error for NVFP4 and 0.590.59–1.05×1.05\times for FP8 across the four models, because SR’s random error is present at full size from the first rounding and grows only in quadrature, while RTN’s bias is small per step but adds linearly and overtakes it once enough steps have accumulated (Appendix C.6). The ratio then rises with NN and crosses one by 16K tokens for FP8 on every model, and on the two GDN models RTN drives the FP8 and NVFP4 state non-finite by 128K and 64K tokens while SR stays finite everywhere. FP16, not tabulated, shows the same crossover on the two Mamba-2 models, where RTN reaches 15×15\times SR on Nemotron-3-Nano-4B at 32K and 2.7×2.7\times on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B at 128K, and stays within 2.3×2.3\times on the GDN models. A checkpoint that is read back into the recurrence therefore needs SR, and a copy that is rounded once and never fed back is better served by RTN.

E.4.6 Downstream accuracy

Protocol.

MMLU-Pro has 12,032 questions, GPQA-Diamond 198 questions with three repetitions, and Math-L5 1,324 questions. Each model uses its recommended sampling settings. The Nemotron models use temperature 1.01.0 and top-pp 0.950.95; Qwen3.5-4B uses temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95, top-kk 2020, and a presence penalty of 1.51.5; Qwen3.5-122B-A10B uses temperature 0.60.6, top-pp 0.950.95, and top-kk 2020. The output budget of each model and benchmark is set near the 99th percentile of the lengths at which FP32 decoding finishes, and a generation that hits the budget counts as wrong, since lenient grading would favor the configurations that truncate most. Every configuration of a model shares the budget, batch size, sampling settings, and per-question seed, and the change from FP32 is computed on the questions the two runs share, so the comparison is paired.

Results.

Table 12 gives the per-model changes behind Table 2 together with the mean and 90th-percentile output length of each cell. Shared FP16+SR and FP8+SR checkpoints stay within benchmark noise of FP32 on every model. The loss of a shared NVFP4+SR checkpoint follows generation length. On every model, GPQA-Diamond has the longest generations of the three benchmarks and also the largest loss, 31.331.3 points on Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, 12.512.5 on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B, 3.23.2 on Qwen3.5-4B, and 5.25.2 on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, against at most 2.92.9 points on MMLU-Pro and Math-L5 for the three larger models. Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, the smallest model, loses 2121 to 4242 points on all three. Part of the GPQA-Diamond loss is failure to finish. On Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B, 20.7%20.7\% of the shared-NVFP4 generations hit the budget against 5.7%5.7\% for FP32, the loss among pairs that both finished is 2.82.8 points, and the length columns show the same with a mean of 28.3K tokens and a 90th percentile at the budget. This is consistent with error that accumulates over a generation (Section 3.3), and Appendix E.4.7 confirms it within each benchmark, where length is not confounded with the benchmark. Separate checkpoints recover most of the loss. With an NVFP4 read and FP16+SR or FP8+SR recurrence, the three larger models stay within 22 points of FP32 on every benchmark, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B still loses 5.65.6 to 6.76.7 points on GPQA-Diamond and 1.51.5 to 2.82.8 elsewhere. GPQA-Diamond has 594 generations per cell and a question-clustered standard error of 2.52.5 to 33 points, so only its larger changes are resolved.

Long input context.

The three benchmarks above test long context on the output side, with prompts of about 1K tokens and generations that reach tens of thousands. RULER-128K (Hsieh et al., 2024) tests it on the input side, with prompts of about 130K tokens and answers of 18 to 81 tokens. Table 13 gives the RULER score of every configuration on its 13 tasks with 100 examples each, under RULER’s protocol of greedy decoding with thinking disabled. Every configuration is within 0.30.3 points of FP32 on every model, a shared NVFP4+SR checkpoint included. This is expected. Quantization applies to decoding only (Section 7.4), so a request here quantizes its post-prefill state once and flushes at most five times, against hundreds to nearly two thousand flushes per request on the reasoning benchmarks. The accuracy loss of a shared low-precision checkpoint therefore appears with long outputs, not with long inputs.

E.4.7 Accuracy by generation length

A single accuracy number does not show where a configuration loses. Figure 14 therefore extends Figure 6 to all four models and three benchmarks and plots accuracy against generation length for the FP32 reference, the shared NVFP4+SR checkpoint, and NVFP4 reads with FP8+SR recurrence. Within each model and benchmark, the bins are quartiles of FP32 output length per question. Each generation is binned by the length of its FP32 counterpart, not its own, since a degraded configuration rambles and would otherwise look long. The FP32 curve comes from a separate FP32 run, because the run that defines the bins puts all of its own truncated generations in the top bin. Each bin is plotted at its median reference length. FP32 accuracy itself falls by 2121 to 5050 points across the bins on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond, since longer generations come from harder questions, so the quantity to read is the gap between a configuration and FP32 within a bin, not the absolute accuracy.

Wherever the shared NVFP4 checkpoint loses accuracy, its gap to FP32 grows with length. On the three larger models it matches FP32 in the short bins and loses in the top bin, by up to 28.228.2 points on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B GPQA-Diamond, and every such top-bin loss comes with more truncation than FP32. On Nemotron-3-Nano-4B it is below FP32 in every bin, with a deficit that grows from 55 to 2929 points on MMLU-Pro and from 88 to 6666 on Math-L5. NVFP4 reads with FP8+SR recurrence stay within the FP32 interval in 41 of the 48 bins.

Appendix F Future work: skipping checkpoint reads by decay

ReplaySSM removes the state write from non-flush steps but still reads the checkpoint at every step, because output computation needs it (Section 4). The checkpoint enters each step only through the cumulative decay. On a non-flush step with hh buffered records the output is

ot=γhSckptqt+∑j=1hγj+1:hvj(kj⊤qt),o_{t}=\gamma_{h}\,S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}\,q_{t}+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\gamma_{j+1:h}\,v_{j}\,(k_{j}^{\top}q_{t}), (18)

and at a flush the new checkpoint is γLSckpt+∑j=1Lγj+1:Lvjkj⊤\gamma_{L}S_{\mathrm{ckpt}}+\sum_{j=1}^{L}\gamma_{j+1:L}v_{j}k_{j}^{\top} (Equation 5). Both checkpoint terms are scaled by a cumulative decay that is data dependent and differs across heads. A head with fast decay reaches a negligible γh\gamma_{h} within a few steps of a window, while a slow-decaying head, which carries information over long horizons, does not.

Once γh\gamma_{h} falls below what the output precision resolves, the checkpoint term can be dropped for that head. A non-flush step then moves only the buffer reads and the record write, and a flush no longer depends on the old checkpoint and becomes a pure write. In the traffic analysis of Appendix C.3, the LL checkpoint reads per window disappear for such a head and leave one checkpoint write plus the buffer traffic, so the state traffic of that head falls well below half of conventional decoding. Since the checkpoint term is scaled by γh\gamma_{h}, a head whose decay is small but not negligible could read a coarser copy of the checkpoint instead of skipping it: the low-precision read checkpoint of Section 6 already provides such a copy, and its rounding error enters the output scaled by γh\gamma_{h}.

Appendix G Adoption

ReplaySSM is adopted in large-scale production models and open-source inference software. GLM-5.3-Flash uses ReplaySSM in its production serving stack (Z.ai, 2026a), and the Z.ai infrastructure report (Z.ai, 2026b) describes adding it to the KDA decode kernel. Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team, 2026) caches the SSM inputs of draft tokens for verification in its KDA layers and cites ReplaySSM as a concurrent approach. ReplaySSM is also integrated into the open-source serving systems TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang and into the kernel library FlashInfer.
